title: Statistical Inference × Causal Inference: A MECE Knowledge Tree
criterion: L1 split criterion: does the target quantity of inference involve an "intervention"?
criterionDetail: Every statistical method answers "what can a sample tell us about the population?"; what differs is the target quantity. If the target is an associational quantity P(Y | X) (a mean, a difference, a conditional relationship), observational data plus sampling assumptions are enough for inference. If the target is an interventional quantity P(Y | do(X)) (how much Y would change if we changed X), we must first specify how the treatment was assigned before the data can "identify" the answer. A target quantity either involves an intervention or it does not, so the two branches are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive.

levels.name: Inference type
levels.rule: Whether the target quantity involves an intervention: associational P(Y | X) / causal P(Y | do(X))

levels.name: Problem type
levels.rule: Statistical inference splits by "the form of the inferential output" (an interval for a quantity / a yes-or-no decision / a model of a conditional relationship); causal inference splits by "the treatment assignment mechanism" (randomized by the researcher / determined by an exogenous rule or event / self-selected by units)

levels.name: Method family
levels.rule: Within each problem type, one single criterion: how uncertainty is quantified, the stage of the testing workflow, the data structure, the main challenge the experiment must overcome, the source of exogenous variation, the target estimand

levels.name: Specific method
levels.rule: Each method appears exactly once, placed by its "most typical use"; uses in other branches are noted on its card

notation: Treatment (D is common in the econometrics literature)
Potential outcomes: the outcome of the same unit with / without treatment
Outcome model E[Y | T = t, X]
Statistical power (here β is the Type II error rate; in regression, β denotes a coefficient)

boundaries.q: Why does logistic regression appear both in the ML knowledge tree and here?
boundaries.a: Same mathematical model, two uses. The ML tree cares about predictive accuracy, and the coefficients are merely a means to that end; the GLM here cares about estimating and drawing inferences on the coefficients themselves (odds ratios, confidence intervals, tests). The two trees use different split criteria, so they offer two perspectives; within any single tree, each method still appears only once.

boundaries.q: The bootstrap and permutation tests both resample; why are they in different branches?
boundaries.a: L2 splits by "the form of the output." The bootstrap produces the sampling distribution of an estimator and a confidence interval (estimation); a permutation test produces a p-value under the null hypothesis (testing). Resampling is only the means, not the split criterion.

boundaries.q: Sequential testing is hypothesis testing; why is it placed under randomized experiments?
boundaries.a: Methodologically it is a test, but in practice it is used almost exclusively to "monitor an experiment continuously and decide when to stop." Under the "most typical use" rule it belongs with experimental design; general-purpose testing methods sit in the "Hypothesis Testing" branch of statistical inference.

boundaries.q: Isn't G-computation just regression? How does it differ from OLS?
boundaries.a: OLS sits under statistical inference, and its target is the coefficient of a conditional relationship; G-computation sits under causal inference, and its target is the difference in mean outcomes under intervention. The two give the same number only when the model has no interactions and all confounding has been adjusted for.

boundaries.q: CUPED also adjusts for covariates; why isn't it under observational adjustment?
boundaries.a: The L2 criterion is the treatment assignment mechanism. CUPED's data come from a randomized experiment, so the covariates serve only to reduce variance and bear no responsibility for removing bias; observational adjustment, by contrast, must rely on covariates to remove confounding, which is a precondition for identification.

boundaries.q: Heterogeneous-effect (CATE) methods are also widely used on experimental data; why are they under observational adjustment?
boundaries.a: At their core, meta-learners and causal forests "adjust via a model": on observational data they require conditional exchangeability, while on experimental data exchangeability is guaranteed automatically by randomization, and the method itself is unchanged. Going by the nature of the method, they sit in the CATE branch under observational adjustment.

boundaries.q: Synthetic control and DiD both use pre-treatment data; how do they differ?
boundaries.a: DiD assumes parallel trends and weights control units equally; synthetic control chooses the control-unit weights by pre-treatment fit and does not need parallel trends, but it requires that the treated unit can be approximated by a weighted average of control units. Both belong to the "time × group" panel-comparison family, and Synthetic DiD combines the two.

boundaries.q: Why isn't causal discovery (the PC algorithm) in this tree?
boundaries.a: This tree covers causal inference of the "treatment and outcome are known; estimate the effect" kind. "Causal discovery," which learns the causal graph among variables from data, outputs a structure of relationships among variables, so under the ML tree's criteria it belongs in "Unsupervised / Variable Relationship Mining." The two are often chained: first draw a DAG from domain knowledge or causal discovery, then estimate the effect with the methods here.

boundaries.q: Does "significant" mean there is a causal effect?
boundaries.a: No. A p-value only answers "if there were truly no difference, how unlikely would a difference this large be?", which is a question of statistical inference. Whether it can be read causally depends on how the treatment was assigned: with a randomized experiment it can; with observational data it must additionally be paired with the identification assumptions of the causal branch on the right.

hybrids: Randomized experiment (causal identification) + Bayesian inference (decisions based on the posterior "probability that B beats A" and on expected loss).
Identification assumptions of observational adjustment + ML-estimated nuisance models + semiparametric theory for confidence intervals.
Randomized experiment data + CATE estimation (meta-learners, causal forests) + targeting decisions ranked by effect.
Random assignment serves as the instrument and actual uptake as the treatment, handling imperfect compliance in experiments (estimates the LATE).
First use matching or weighting to make the two groups' pre-treatment characteristics similar, then run DiD, so that the parallel-trends assumption is more credible.

children.name: Statistical Inference (Associational)
children.signal: The target quantity is an associational P(Y | X) or a population parameter: infer the population from a sample and quantify the uncertainty, without claiming any effect of an intervention.
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: the form of the inferential output (an interval for a quantity / a yes-or-no decision / a model of a conditional relationship)

children.name: Parameter Estimation & Uncertainty
children.def: Output: a point estimate and an interval for a parameter (confidence or credible interval), answering "how much, and how uncertain?"
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: how uncertainty is quantified (analytic approximation / computational resampling / probabilistic prior)

children.name: Frequentist Analytic Methods
children.philosophy: Treat the estimator as a random variable, derive its sampling distribution from large-sample theory (the central limit theorem, asymptotic normality), and obtain a confidence interval from it.

leaves.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
leaves.zh: Estimating parameters by maximizing the likelihood
leaves.plain: Think of it in reverse: "What parameter value would be most likely to produce the data I actually have?" Then pick that value. For example, if a coin lands heads 7 times in 10 tosses, the most reasonable guess for the probability of heads is 0.7. It is the common principle behind parameter estimation in most statistical models.
leaves.intuition: Choose the parameter values under which the observed data are "most likely." In large samples the MLE is asymptotically unbiased and asymptotically normal, and its variance attains the theoretical lower bound (Cramér–Rao), so standard errors can be computed directly from the curvature of the likelihood (the Fisher information): the more sharply curved the likelihood, the more precise the estimate.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\theta} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}\, \ell(\theta)$
$\qquad = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(x_i \mid \theta)$
Asymptotic distribution: $\hat{\theta} \approx \mathcal{N}\big(\theta,\, \mathcal{I}(\theta)^{-1}\big)$
$\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial \theta^2}\right]$
Wald interval: $\hat{\theta} \pm z_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \operatorname{SE}(\hat{\theta})$
assumptions: Model (distributional family) correctly specified
Observations are independent and identically distributed
Parameters are identifiable, and the true value is not on the boundary of the parameter space
Sample is large enough (for the asymptotic results to hold)
checks: Check the distributional assumption with residual plots and QQ plots
Compare nested models with likelihood-ratio tests
In small samples, cross-check intervals against the bootstrap
Check whether the likelihood is too flat (identification problems)
pros: Consistent and asymptotically efficient
Unified framework for estimation and testing (Wald, likelihood ratio, score)
Foundation of generalized linear models and survival models
use: Coefficient estimation in generalized linear models
Fitting distribution parameters (e.g., a Gamma distribution for claim amounts)
Likelihood-ratio tests
cons: Estimates can be biased when the model is misspecified
Asymptotic approximations are inaccurate in small samples
May have multiple local maxima; requires numerical optimization
hp: Numerical optimization is sensitive to starting values; method-of-moments estimates make a good starting point
Use robust (sandwich) standard errors when the model may be misspecified
Use profile-likelihood intervals or the bootstrap instead
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.<distribution>.fit, statsmodels GenericLikelihoodModel; R: stats4::mle, MASS::fitdistr

leaves.name: Confidence Intervals (CLT / t-Distribution)
leaves.plain: A sample mean is only an estimate; a different sample would give a different number. A confidence interval gives a range, e.g., "conversion rate 5.2%, 95% confidence interval 4.8%–5.6%." The key point: the narrower the interval, the more precise the estimate, and quadrupling the sample size roughly halves the interval width.
leaves.intuition: The sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal (central limit theorem), so "the mean ± about 2 standard errors" covers the true value with roughly 95% probability. Interpret it with care: 95% refers to the long-run coverage rate of the procedure, not the probability that the true value lies in this particular interval.
leaves.objective:
Mean: $\bar{x} \pm t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$
Proportion (Wilson interval; better than Wald for small samples or proportions near 0 or 1):
$\frac{\hat{p} + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}}$
assumptions: Observations are independent
Sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to apply (the more skewed the distribution, the larger the sample needed)
The t interval assumes approximately normal data or a large sample
checks: Check skewness and outliers (convergence is slow for heavy-tailed distributions)
Switch to Wilson or exact intervals when the proportion is near 0 or 1
Verify actual coverage by simulation
pros: Simple and easy to communicate
Conveys both effect size and uncertainty, so it is more informative than a p-value alone
use: Margins of error for reported metrics
Effect intervals in A/B tests
Margins of error for survey proportions
cons: Often misread as "a 95% probability that the true value is in the interval"
Actual coverage falls short for heavy-tailed metrics (e.g., revenue)
Standard errors are underestimated when data are dependent (clustered data, time series)
hp: 95% by convention, but choose it based on decision costs
Consider winsorizing, a log transform, or the bootstrap
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.t.interval, statsmodels.stats.proportion.proportion_confint; R: t.test, binom::binom.confint

leaves.name: Delta Method
leaves.zh: Standard errors via first-order Taylor expansion
leaves.plain: Many metrics are ratios or other transformations, such as revenue per user (total revenue ÷ number of users) or the log of a proportion. The delta method uses an approximation that "treats a curve as a straight line over a small range" to carry the uncertainty of the underlying variables over to these metrics and compute their standard errors.
leaves.intuition: When the quantity you care about is a function of an estimator, such as the ratio metric "clicks per user = total clicks ÷ total users," linearize the function with a first-order Taylor expansion and derive its approximate variance from the variance of the original estimator. In A/B testing, standard errors for ratio metrics are commonly computed this way.
leaves.objective:
$\sqrt{n}\,\big(g(\hat{\theta}) - g(\theta)\big)$
$\qquad \to \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ \nabla g(\theta)^\top \Sigma\, \nabla g(\theta)\big)$
For the ratio $R = \bar{X} / \bar{Y}$:
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat{R}) \approx \frac{1}{\mu_Y^2} \big[\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X})$
$\qquad - 2R \operatorname{Cov}(\bar{X}, \bar{Y}) + R^2 \operatorname{Var}(\bar{Y})\big]$
assumptions: The function g is differentiable at the true value, with a nonzero derivative
The original estimator is asymptotically normal
Sample is large enough for the first-order approximation to be accurate
checks: Cross-check delta-method standard errors against the bootstrap
Check whether the denominator mean is close to 0 (the ratio becomes very unstable)
pros: Closed-form and fast to compute
Well suited to ratio metrics in large-scale online experiments
use: Ratio metrics in A/B tests (CTR, revenue per user)
Standard errors of transformed parameters such as log odds and elasticities
cons: Approximation is inaccurate in small samples or under strong nonlinearity
Requires correctly estimated covariances
hp: Aggregate both the numerator and the denominator of a ratio metric by the "randomization unit" before computing
Validate the standard errors with an A/A test or the bootstrap before launch
leaves.tools: Python: compute by hand, or use statsmodels regression results with numerical gradients; R: msm::deltamethod

children.name: Resampling Methods
children.philosophy: Rather than deriving formulas, repeatedly resample from the data by computer to simulate the estimator's sampling distribution directly.

leaves.name: Bootstrap
leaves.plain: You can quantify uncertainty without memorizing formulas: resample your data "with replacement" a few thousand times, recompute the metric each time, and see how spread out the results are; that tells you how unstable the estimate is. It is especially handy for metrics like medians and ratios that have no simple formula.
leaves.intuition: Treat the sample as a miniature of the population: draw new samples of the same size from it "with replacement" and recompute the statistic thousands of times; the distribution of these results approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic. Any complex statistic (a median, a difference in quantiles, a model metric) can get an interval through the same procedure.
leaves.objective:
Repeat $B$ times: let $x^{*(b)}$ be a resample drawn with replacement from $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$, of size $n$, and compute $\hat{\theta}^{*(b)}$
Percentile interval: $\big[\hat{\theta}^*_{(\alpha/2)},\ \hat{\theta}^*_{(1-\alpha/2)}\big]$
The BCa interval additionally corrects for bias and skewness
assumptions: The sample is representative of the population
Observations are independent (dependent data require a block or cluster bootstrap)
The statistic is a smooth function of the data (it may fail for extreme-value statistics such as the maximum)
checks: Increase B and confirm the interval is stable
Compare percentile and BCa intervals (a large difference signals skewness or bias)
Use a block bootstrap for time series and check sensitivity to the block length
pros: Applies to almost any statistic
No distributional assumptions required
Intuitive and easy to implement
use: Metrics without simple formulas, such as medians, quantiles, and ratios
Intervals for model evaluation metrics (AUC, QWK)
A/B tests on non-normal metrics
cons: Computationally intensive
In small samples the sample itself is poorly representative, so intervals tend to be too narrow
Extreme-value statistics and dependent data require specialized variants
hp: At least 2,000 for interval estimation; about 200 is enough if you only need standard errors
Cluster bootstrap for clustered data; block bootstrap for time series
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.bootstrap; R: boot

children.name: Bayesian Inference
children.philosophy: Treat the parameter as a random variable: prior × likelihood = posterior, which directly answers "what is the probability that the parameter lies in a given range?"

leaves.name: Conjugate Bayes (Beta-Binomial)
leaves.plain: Start with an "initial belief" (the prior) and, after seeing data, update it to a "new belief" (the posterior). The Beta-Binomial update is especially simple: the prior acts like "having already seen a few successes and a few failures," and the new data are simply added on. It can directly answer "What is the probability that version B is better than version A?"
leaves.intuition: The prior and the posterior belong to the same distributional family, so updating only requires adding up counts. For a conversion rate, use Beta(α, β) as the prior; after observing s successes and f failures, the posterior is Beta(α + s, β + f). You can directly compute "the probability that version B's conversion rate is higher than A's," and the prior can also encode historical experience, making estimates more stable in small samples.
leaves.objective:
Prior $p \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$; data: $s$ successes and $f$ failures
Posterior $p \mid \text{data} \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha + s,\, \beta + f)$
Posterior mean $= \frac{\alpha + s}{\alpha + \beta + s + f}$
$\mathbb{P}(p_B > p_A \mid \text{data})$ is estimated by sampling from the posterior
assumptions: Likelihood correctly specified (e.g., independent Bernoulli trials)
The prior is reasonable and chosen before looking at the data
checks: Prior sensitivity analysis: try different priors and see whether the conclusions change
Posterior predictive checks
pros: Extremely cheap to compute; can be updated in real time
Intuitive results (direct probability statements)
The prior can incorporate historical information, stabilizing small-sample estimates
use: Bayesian A/B testing
Conversion-rate estimation with small samples, such as new or long-tail products
Posterior updates in Thompson Sampling
cons: Only works for a handful of conjugate pairs
The choice of prior is subjective and should be disclosed
A high "probability that B beats A" does not mean the effect is large enough
hp: α + β acts as a "pseudo sample size"; usually set it small (e.g., 1–10) or estimate it from historical data
Pair it with an expected-loss threshold rather than looking only at the win probability
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.beta, PyMC; R: bayesAB

leaves.name: MCMC (HMC / NUTS)
leaves.plain: Complex Bayesian models usually have no formula for the posterior. MCMC uses a clever random walk that "lingers where probability is high" in parameter space; after walking long enough, the path it leaves behind represents the posterior distribution. HMC/NUTS uses the slope of the terrain to move more efficiently.
leaves.intuition: Most posterior distributions have no closed form. MCMC constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is exactly the posterior, then approximates the posterior with draws from the chain. Modern HMC/NUTS uses gradient information to glide through parameter space like a physical particle, making it far more efficient than a random walk in high-dimensional models.
leaves.objective:
Goal: sample from $p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(y \mid \theta) \cdot p(\theta)$
Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability:
$a = \min\left(1,\ \frac{p(\theta' \mid y)\, q(\theta \mid \theta')}{p(\theta \mid y)\, q(\theta' \mid \theta)}\right)$
HMC: proposes candidates via Hamiltonian dynamics with $H(\theta, r) = -\log p(\theta \mid y) + \frac{1}{2} r^\top M^{-1} r$
assumptions: The chain has converged to its stationary distribution
The effective sample size is large enough to represent the posterior
Model specification and priors are reasonable
checks: R̂ (Gelman-Rubin) below 1.01
Sufficient effective sample size (ESS), e.g., above 400
No divergent transitions in NUTS
Trace plots and posterior predictive checks
pros: Can fit almost any probabilistic model
Yields the full posterior distribution, not just a point estimate
Naturally handles hierarchical structure and missing values
use: Complex Bayesian models (hierarchical models, marketing mix models/MMM)
Propagating uncertainty into downstream decisions
Problems with little data but rich domain knowledge
cons: Slow to compute and hard to scale to large data (variational inference is an alternative)
Convergence diagnostics take experience
Poor parameterizations make sampling difficult and call for reparameterization
hp: At least 4 chains; start from 1,000 warmup and 1,000 sampling iterations
Use a non-centered parameterization for hierarchical models
leaves.tools: Python: PyMC, NumPyro, CmdStanPy; R: brms, rstan

leaves.name: Hierarchical Bayes (Partial Pooling)
leaves.plain: You have many small groups (stores, regions, schools), each with a different amount of data. Estimating each one separately makes the small groups very unstable; lumping everything together ignores real differences. A hierarchical model strikes a compromise: groups with little data "borrow strength" more from the overall average, while groups with lots of data mostly trust their own.
leaves.intuition: With many groups (stores, products, regions), fully separate estimates are dominated by noise from the small groups, while complete pooling ignores between-group differences. A hierarchical model lets each group's parameter come from a common parent distribution: groups with many observations mostly trust their own data, while groups with few are "pulled toward" the overall mean (shrinkage).
leaves.objective:
$y_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_j, \sigma^2)$, $\theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2)$, with separate priors on $\mu$ and $\tau$
Posterior mean $\approx \frac{\frac{n_j}{\sigma^2}\, \bar{y}_j + \frac{1}{\tau^2}\, \mu}{\frac{n_j}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau^2}}$
The larger the sample size $n_j$, the more weight goes to the group's own mean $\bar{y}_j$
assumptions: Groups are exchangeable: no prior reason to believe any particular group is special
The group-level distribution is reasonably specified
checks: Compare the predictive performance of complete pooling, no pooling, and partial pooling (LOO-CV)
Examine the posterior of τ: values near 0 indicate little between-group variation
pros: More stable estimates for small groups
Automatically determines how much information to borrow from the whole
Also estimates how large the group differences are
use: Conversion-rate or sales estimates across many stores or products
Small-area estimation
Combining results from multiple A/B tests (meta-analysis)
cons: Requires MCMC; computationally expensive
Shrinkage introduces bias when groups are not exchangeable
Harder to explain to non-technical audiences
hp: Use a non-centered parameterization when there are many groups or little data
Use a weakly informative prior such as a half-normal or half-Cauchy
leaves.tools: Python: PyMC, Bambi; R: brms (lme4 as a frequentist approximation)

children.name: Hypothesis Testing
children.def: Output: a decision on the null hypothesis (reject or fail to reject) and a p-value, answering "does the difference or association really exist, or is it just sampling noise?"
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the stage of the testing workflow being addressed (pre-study design / parametric tests / nonparametric tests / multiple comparisons)

children.name: Pre-study Design
children.philosophy: Decide, before collecting any data, how large an effect you want to detect and how many observations you need, so you avoid "claiming no difference from an underpowered sample."

leaves.name: Power Analysis & Sample Size
leaves.plain: Before the experiment starts, work out: "How large a sample do I need to be reasonably sure of detecting the effect I care about?" The smaller the effect and the noisier the data, the larger the sample you need. With too small a sample, even a real effect will likely go unnoticed, and the experiment is wasted.
leaves.intuition: Statistical power is "the probability of detecting an effect when it truly exists." Sample size, effect size, noise, and significance level constrain one another: fix any three and you can solve for the fourth. In practice you usually set the minimum detectable effect (MDE) first, i.e., the effect below which it is not worth taking action, and then compute the required sample size.
leaves.objective:
Comparing two means (sample size per group):
$n \approx \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\, \sigma^2}{\delta^2}$
Comparing two proportions:
$n \approx \frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{(p_1 - p_2)^2}$
$\qquad \times \big[\,p_1(1-p_1) + p_2(1-p_2)\,\big]$
Common choices: $\alpha = 0.05$, power $1 - \beta = 0.8$
assumptions: The prior estimate of the variance σ² is reliable (usually from historical data)
The MDE reflects the smallest effect that matters to the business
The test used for planning matches the one used in the actual analysis
checks: Don't compute post hoc "observed power" (it maps one-to-one to the p-value and adds no information)
Confirm the variance estimate with A/A tests or simulations on historical data
pros: Avoids false negatives caused by insufficient sample size
Makes experiment duration and cost plannable
Turns "how small an effect is worth caring about" into an explicit business decision
use: Estimating how many days an A/B test needs to run before launch
Sample planning for clinical trials or market surveys
Judging whether an effect is detectable in practice at all
cons: Depends on the variance estimate; if it is wrong, the sample will be too small
Setting the MDE too small makes experiments impractically long
hp: Set it by business value, e.g., +0.5 percentage points in conversion rate
CUPED can substantially reduce the required sample size
Adjust α as the number of groups grows (see Multiple Testing Correction)
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels.stats.power (TTestIndPower, NormalIndPower); R: pwr

children.name: Parametric & Large-Sample Tests
children.philosophy: Assume the test statistic follows a known distribution (t, F, χ², normal) and compute the p-value from it; with a large enough sample, most of these hold by the central limit theorem.

leaves.name: Welch's t-Test
leaves.plain: Checks whether the difference between two groups' averages is too large to be just luck. Welch's version doesn't require the two groups to have the same spread, so it is more robust than the classic t-test and should be the default in practice.
leaves.intuition: Compares the difference between two group means with the noise in the estimate of that difference. Welch's version does not assume equal variances and should be the default in practice; with large enough samples it is approximately valid even when the data are not normal.
leaves.objective:
$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$
Degrees of freedom (Welch–Satterthwaite):
$\nu \approx \frac{(s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2)^2}{\frac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \frac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}$
assumptions: Independent observations (within and between groups)
Sample means approximately normal (large enough samples, or approximately normal data)
checks: Check for outliers and heavy tails (very common in revenue metrics)
Use a paired t-test for paired data
Correct the standard errors when randomizing by user but analyzing at the event level
pros: Simple, fast, and widely known
Robust to non-normal data in large samples
use: Continuous metrics in A/B tests (time on page, average order value)
Comparing results between two experimental groups
cons: Sensitive to outliers
Unreliable with small, highly skewed samples
Underestimates variance when the unit of analysis differs from the unit of randomization
hp: Don't run an equal-variance test first to decide which t-test to use (the two-stage procedure distorts α)
Winsorize, log-transform, or switch to a nonparametric test or the bootstrap
Decide in advance; two-sided is the usual choice
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=False); R: t.test

leaves.name: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
leaves.plain: When comparing the averages of three or more groups, it runs a single test of whether "at least one group is different," instead of running t-tests on every pair (running too many raises the chance of a false alarm). It works by comparing the differences between groups with the variation that naturally exists within each group.
leaves.intuition: Compares the means of three or more groups: if the differences among group means (between-group variance) are much larger than the random fluctuation within groups (within-group variance), at least one group differs. It tests all groups at once, avoiding the Type I error inflation of pairwise t-tests; once a difference is confirmed, follow up with post hoc comparisons.
leaves.objective:
$F = \frac{\mathrm{SS}_{\text{between}} / (k - 1)}{\mathrm{SS}_{\text{within}} / (N - k)}$
$\qquad \sim F(k - 1,\, N - k)$
$\mathrm{SS}_{\text{between}} = \sum_{j} n_j (\bar{x}_j - \bar{x})^2$
$\mathrm{SS}_{\text{within}} = \sum_{j} \sum_{i} (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2$
assumptions: Independent observations
Residuals approximately normal within each group
Equal variances across groups (use Welch's ANOVA if not)
checks: Residual QQ plot
Levene's test, or simply compare the groups' standard deviations
If significant, use Tukey's HSD for post hoc pairwise comparisons
pros: Compares many groups at once while controlling the overall Type I error
Extends to multiple factors and interactions (factorial designs)
use: Multi-variant experiments (A/B/C/D)
Factorial experiments (price × copy)
Comparing processes or formulations
cons: Only tells you that a difference exists, not which group differs
Not robust when variances and group sizes are both unequal
hp: Tukey's HSD for all pairwise comparisons; Dunnett's test when every group is compared with the control
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.f_oneway, statsmodels anova_lm, pingouin; R: aov, car::Anova

leaves.name: Chi-Square Test of Independence
leaves.zh: Test of association for contingency tables
leaves.plain: Checks whether two categorical variables are related, such as "plan type" and "whether the customer renews." First work out how many people each cell "should" have if the two were completely unrelated, then see how far the actual numbers deviate. The larger the deviation, the less it looks like there is no relationship.
leaves.intuition: Tests whether two categorical variables are independent: first compute "how many observations each cell should have if the two were independent," then measure how far the observed counts deviate from these expected counts. The larger the deviation, the less likely the variables are independent.
leaves.objective:
$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$
$E_{ij} = \frac{\text{row } i \text{ total} \times \text{column } j \text{ total}}{N}$
Degrees of freedom $= (r - 1)(c - 1)$
Effect size: Cramér's $V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{N\,(\min(r, c) - 1)}}$
assumptions: Independent observations (each individual counted only once)
Expected counts large enough (common rule of thumb: at least 5 per cell)
checks: Use Fisher's exact test when expected counts are too small
Examine standardized residuals to find which cells deviate the most
pros: Works with categorical data
Simple, intuitive, and handles many categories
use: Whether preferences differ across customer segments
Comparing conversion rates in A/B tests (2×2 table)
Survey cross-tabulation
cons: Tests only whether there is an association, not its direction or size (report an effect size separately)
With very large samples, even tiny differences become significant
hp: Use Fisher's exact test for 2×2 tables with small expected counts
Always report Cramér's V or the difference in proportions
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.chi2_contingency, fisher_exact; R: chisq.test, fisher.test

children.name: Nonparametric & Resampling Tests
children.philosophy: Make no assumption about the shape of the data distribution; instead, build the null distribution from ranks or by permuting the labels.

leaves.name: Mann-Whitney U Test
leaves.plain: Instead of comparing averages, it pools all the values from both groups, ranks them, and checks whether one group generally ranks higher. It isn't thrown off by extreme values and doesn't require a normal distribution, so it suits heavily skewed data such as revenue.
leaves.intuition: Pool the two groups, rank all the values, and check whether one group's ranks are systematically higher. It tests whether "the probability that a random value from A exceeds a random value from B is 50%," and it is insensitive to outliers.
leaves.objective:
$U = R_1 - \frac{n_1(n_1 + 1)}{2}$ ($R_1$ is the sum of ranks in group 1)
Effect size: $\text{AUC} = \frac{U}{n_1 n_2} = \mathbb{P}(X_A > X_B)$ (ties count as $\frac{1}{2}$)
assumptions: Independent observations
Data at least on an ordinal scale
To interpret the result as a "difference in medians," the two distributions must have the same shape
checks: Compare the shapes of the two distributions (if they differ, the conclusion is about stochastic dominance, not a difference in medians)
Use the tie-corrected version when there are many ties
pros: Robust to outliers and skewness
No normality assumption
Exact distribution available for small samples
use: Comparing heavy-tailed metrics (revenue, usage time)
Ordinal data such as satisfaction ratings
Two-group comparisons with small samples
cons: Often mistaken for a test of medians
Gives only a p-value; the effect size must be reported separately
Slightly less powerful than the t-test when the data are normal
hp: Report the AUC or the Hodges–Lehmann shift estimate
Use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test instead
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu; R: wilcox.test

leaves.name: Permutation Test
leaves.plain: If the treatment truly has no effect, the labels saying who belongs to which group could be swapped at will. Shuffle the labels thousands of times and see how rare the difference you actually observed is among the shuffled results. It needs almost no distributional assumptions, and the logic is very intuitive.
leaves.intuition: If the treatment truly has no effect, the group labels can be swapped freely. Randomly shuffle the labels thousands of times, recomputing the statistic each time, to get "the distribution of the statistic when there is no effect," then see how extreme the observed value is within it. Any statistic can be tested this way.
leaves.objective:
$p = \frac{1 + \#\{\, b : T(\pi_b(\mathcal{D})) \ge T(\mathcal{D}) \,\}}{B + 1}$
$\mathcal{D}$ is the data; $\pi_b$ is the random permutation of the labels in draw $b$
assumptions: Labels are exchangeable under the null hypothesis (automatically true in randomized experiments)
Permute at the correct unit (permute whole clusters for clustered data)
checks: The number of permutations B is large enough for a stable p-value
In stratified or clustered designs, permute in a way that mirrors the original randomization
pros: Needs almost no distributional assumptions and controls the Type I error exactly
Works for any statistic (difference in medians, quantiles, custom metrics)
Consistent with the logic of randomized experiments
use: A/B tests on non-normal metrics
Small-sample experiments
Testing custom composite metrics
cons: Computationally intensive
Not applicable to observational data where labels are not exchangeable
Provides only a test; intervals require the bootstrap or test inversion
hp: At least 5,000–10,000; more if you need to report very small p-values
Decide in advance; don't pick one after seeing the results
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.permutation_test; R: coin, perm

leaves.name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov Test
leaves.plain: Checks whether two datasets have the same "overall distribution shape," not just the same average. It looks at the biggest gap between the two cumulative distribution curves. It is also commonly used to check whether a model's feature distributions have drifted.
leaves.intuition: Tests whether two distributions are the same overall: plot the cumulative distribution curves of both groups and find the largest vertical distance between them. The larger the distance, the less likely the two come from the same distribution. It looks beyond the mean, detecting differences in location, shape, and spread.
leaves.objective:
$D = \sup_x \big|\hat{F}_1(x) - \hat{F}_2(x)\big|$
In large samples, $\sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}} \cdot D$ follows the Kolmogorov distribution
assumptions: Independent observations
Continuous distributions (conservative for discrete data with many ties)
checks: Plot both ECDFs to see where the differences occur
For discrete data, use a chi-square or permutation test instead
pros: Detects any kind of distributional difference
No distributional assumptions required
use: Data drift detection (comparing training and production data distributions)
Checking randomization in A/A tests
Comparing model score distributions
cons: Sensitive in the middle of the distribution but not in the tails (use Anderson–Darling for the tails)
With very large samples, even tiny differences become significant
hp: Look at the size of D as well, not just the p-value
leaves.tools: Python: scipy.stats.ks_2samp; R: ks.test

children.name: Multiple Comparisons Correction
children.philosophy: When many tests are run at once, the probability of at least one false positive inflates quickly, so the thresholds must be adjusted to control the overall error rate.

leaves.name: Bonferroni / Holm (FWER Control)
leaves.plain: When you run many tests at once, it is easy to "hit" one or two false positives even if none of the effects are real. Bonferroni divides the significance threshold by the number of tests, which is very conservative; Holm is an improved version that relaxes the threshold step by step. It keeps the same control over the chance of making even a single error, but finds real effects more easily.
leaves.intuition: With 20 tests at α = 5% each, the probability of at least one false positive is about 64%. Bonferroni divides the threshold by the number of tests; Holm's step-down version starts from the smallest p-value and checks each in turn against a progressively looser threshold. It gives the same guarantee that the probability of "at least one false positive" does not exceed α, but with higher power.
leaves.objective:
$\text{FWER} = \mathbb{P}(\text{at least one false positive}) \le \alpha$
Bonferroni: reject when $p_i \le \alpha / m$
Holm: order the $p$-values as $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}$
If $p_{(k)} \le \frac{\alpha}{m - k + 1}$, reject and continue; otherwise stop
assumptions: Tests need not be independent; valid under any dependence structure
checks: List all hypotheses to be tested in advance to avoid post hoc cherry-picking
pros: Strong guarantee: controls FWER under any dependence structure
Holm is always at least as powerful as Bonferroni
use: A small number of primary metrics in an experiment
Decisions that must be very conservative (medical, regulatory)
cons: Overly conservative when there are many tests, with a sharp loss of power
hp: Apply FWER correction to primary metrics only; label secondary metrics as exploratory
When you need FWER control, simply use Holm instead of Bonferroni
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(method='holm'); R: p.adjust(method='holm')

leaves.name: Benjamini–Hochberg (FDR Control)
leaves.plain: Instead of demanding "not a single mistake," it controls "what share of the results you call real are actually false" (for example, no more than 5%). In exploratory settings where you test hundreds of metrics or genes at once, it finds real effects much more readily than Bonferroni.
leaves.intuition: With many tests (hundreds of metrics, thousands of genes), requiring "not a single false positive" is too strict. FDR instead controls "the proportion of false positives among the results declared significant," e.g., 10%: on average, at most one in ten of all findings declared significant is false.
leaves.objective:
$\text{FDR} = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\text{number of false positives}}{\text{number of rejections}}\right]$
BH: sort the $p$-values in ascending order and find the largest $k$ such that $p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{m} \cdot q$
Reject $p_{(1)}, \dots, p_{(k)}$
assumptions: Tests are independent or positively correlated; under arbitrary dependence, use the more conservative Benjamini–Yekutieli instead
checks: Define the scope of the "family" of tests (which tests are corrected together)
pros: Retains power even with a very large number of tests
Easy to interpret (the share of false positives among discoveries)
use: Experiment dashboards with many metrics
Large-scale screening, e.g., genomics or ad keywords
Feature screening
cons: No guarantee of zero false positives
Control can break down under strong negative correlation between tests
hp: Define it in advance and keep it fixed
leaves.tools: Python: multipletests(method='fdr_bh'); R: p.adjust(method='BH')

children.name: Associational Modeling
children.def: Output: a statistical model of the conditional relationship E[Y | X], plus inference on its coefficients (standard errors, intervals, tests), answering "after controlling for other variables, how strong is the association between X and Y?"
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: data structure and response type (independent observations / dependent or clustered data / time to event)

children.name: Linear & Generalized Linear Models
children.philosophy: Model the conditional mean with a linear structure (after transformation by a link function); the focus is on estimating the coefficients and their uncertainty.

leaves.name: OLS with Robust Standard Errors
leaves.zh: Ordinary Least Squares with Robust SE
leaves.plain: The most widely used regression: draw the line that minimizes the sum of squared errors, and read off each variable's average effect. "Robust standard errors" correct how the uncertainty is calculated, so confidence intervals and p-values stay trustworthy even when the size of the errors varies or observations are related to each other.
leaves.intuition: OLS finds the line (hyperplane) that minimizes the residual sum of squares; a coefficient means "how much Y changes on average when X increases by one unit, holding the other variables fixed." In real data the error variance is usually not constant (heteroskedasticity), so inference should use robust (sandwich) standard errors; otherwise the confidence intervals will be too narrow.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$
Heteroskedasticity-robust covariance:
$\hat{V} = (X^\top X)^{-1} \left(\sum_{i} \hat{\varepsilon}_i^2\, x_i x_i^\top\right) (X^\top X)^{-1}$
Cluster-robust: replace the middle term with the outer products of the scores summed within each cluster
assumptions: Linear in parameters
Exogeneity: E[ε | X] = 0 (omitting important variables causes bias)
No perfect collinearity
Independent observations (otherwise use cluster-robust standard errors)
checks: Residuals vs. fitted values plot (nonlinearity, heteroskedasticity)
Check collinearity with VIF
Add or remove control variables and see whether the coefficients are stable
pros: Interpretable and fast
Robust standard errors keep inference valid under heteroskedasticity
Common foundation for econometric methods such as DiD and IV
use: Association analysis controlling for other factors
Descriptive analysis of price elasticity and marketing effects
Estimation tool within causal designs
cons: Coefficients can be interpreted causally only when exogeneity holds
Sensitive to outliers
The linearity assumption may be too strong
hp: Default to HC3 (small samples) or cluster-robust standard errors
Consider logging skewed variables so coefficients can be read as elasticities
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels OLS(...).fit(cov_type='HC3' or 'cluster'); R: lm + sandwich + lmtest

leaves.name: Generalized Linear Models (Logistic / Poisson)
leaves.plain: Use it when the outcome isn't a normally distributed continuous number: yes/no (logistic regression) or counts (Poisson regression). It maps the linear model's output onto a sensible range (probabilities between 0 and 1, counts that can't be negative), and the coefficients can be read as odds ratios or multiplicative changes.
leaves.intuition: When Y is binary, a count, or positively skewed, a plain linear model is a poor fit. A GLM uses a link function to map the mean onto a scale that can be modeled linearly (log-odds, log) and pairs it with an appropriate distribution family. Exponentiated coefficients can be interpreted as odds ratios (logistic) or rate ratios (Poisson).
leaves.objective:
$g\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\big) = X\beta$, where $Y$ follows an exponential-family distribution
Logistic: $\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = X\beta$; $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the odds ratio
Poisson: $\log \mathbb{E}[Y] = X\beta + \log(\text{exposure})$
$\exp(\beta_j)$ is the rate ratio
assumptions: Link function and distribution family are reasonably specified
Independent observations
Poisson assumes the mean equals the variance (often violated in practice)
checks: Test for overdispersion (if residual deviance ÷ degrees of freedom is much greater than 1, switch to negative binomial)
Check calibration plots for logistic models
Consider zero-inflated models when there are excess zeros
pros: Coefficients have a clear multiplicative interpretation
Handles many types of response variables
Estimated by MLE, with a complete inference framework
use: Risk factor analysis (odds ratios)
Event count analysis (number of claims, complaints)
Actuarial science and epidemiology
cons: Standard errors are underestimated under overdispersion
Odds ratios are often misread as risk ratios
Estimates diverge under complete separation
hp: Switch to negative binomial or quasi-Poisson
Include an offset for count data (e.g., policy-years)
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels GLM, smf.logit, smf.poisson; R: glm, MASS::glm.nb
leaves.note: Logistic regression also appears in the ML knowledge tree (supervised / tabular data / regularized linear models), where the goal is predictive accuracy; here the goal is estimation of and inference on the coefficients. Same mathematical model, framed as a different learning problem.

children.name: Dependent & Clustered Data
children.philosophy: Observations from the same cluster (store, user, school) or repeated measurements on the same unit are correlated; ignore that correlation and the standard errors will be too small.

leaves.name: Mixed-Effects Models
leaves.plain: Use it when the data have a group structure, such as the same student taking several exams or the same store observed over many months. The model estimates both the overall average effect and each group's own deviation, and it doesn't treat data from the same group as independent observations, so the conclusions are more reliable.
leaves.intuition: It splits the effect into two parts: fixed effects shared by all groups, and a random offset for each group. The random effects are assumed to come from a common distribution, so estimates for small groups are shrunk toward the overall mean (the same idea as hierarchical Bayes), while within-group correlation is properly accounted for.
leaves.objective:
$y_{ij} = x_{ij}^\top \beta + z_{ij}^\top u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}$
$u_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, G)$, $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$
Variance components estimated by REML
Intraclass correlation coefficient $\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}$
assumptions: Random effects are normal and uncorrelated with the covariates (otherwise biased; use fixed effects or the Mundlak correction instead)
Enough groups (estimating variance components usually needs at least 20–30 groups)
checks: Use the ICC to gauge the degree of clustering
Compare random-intercept and random-slope models (AIC, likelihood ratio)
Compare fixed and random effects with a Hausman test
pros: Properly handles repeated measures and clustered structure
Estimates group differences and the overall effect together
Works with unbalanced data
use: Sales analysis across multiple stores or regions
Analysis of repeated user behavior
Multilevel data in education and healthcare
cons: Many specification choices; results can be sensitive to them
Variance component estimates are unstable with too few groups
Convergence problems are common
hp: Start with random intercepts; add random slopes only with theoretical justification
Use ML when comparing fixed effects and REML when reporting variance components
Standardize covariates and simplify the random-effects structure
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels MixedLM, Bambi; R: lme4, glmmTMB

leaves.name: Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE)
leaves.plain: It also handles repeated measures or grouped data, but cares only about the overall average effect rather than describing how each group differs. It is forgiving about the assumed within-group correlation structure: even if you get it wrong, the standard errors are still usable.
leaves.intuition: Rather than modeling a random effect for each group, it directly estimates the "overall average" relationship (the population-averaged effect), then handles within-group correlation with a working correlation structure plus robust standard errors. Even if the correlation structure is misspecified, the coefficients and robust standard errors remain consistent.
leaves.objective:
$\sum_{j} D_j^\top V_j^{-1} \big(y_j - \mu_j(\beta)\big) = 0$
$V_j = A_j^{1/2} R(\alpha) A_j^{1/2}$
Robust standard errors computed with the sandwich estimator
assumptions: Correctly specified mean model
Groups are independent of one another
Enough groups (robust standard errors are a large-sample result)
Missing data are missing completely at random (MCAR)
checks: Compare results across working correlation structures (independence, exchangeable, AR1)
Use small-sample-corrected standard errors when there are few groups
pros: Robust to misspecification of the correlation structure
Coefficients are population-averaged effects, well suited to policy questions
use: Binary or count outcomes with repeated measures
Policy analysis that needs population-averaged effects
cons: No individual-level predictions
Standard errors are unreliable with few groups
Stronger assumptions about the missing-data mechanism than mixed models
hp: Choose exchangeable or AR1 based on the structure of the data
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels GEE; R: geepack

children.name: Survival Analysis
children.philosophy: The outcome is "how long until the event occurs," and some units have not yet had the event when observation ends (censoring); this incomplete information must be used correctly.

leaves.name: Kaplan–Meier Estimator
leaves.zh: Product-limit estimator of the survival function
leaves.plain: Estimates the share of people still "surviving" (not yet churned) up to each point in time, drawn as a staircase curve that steps down. It correctly handles people for whom the event hasn't happened by the end of observation (e.g., customers who haven't canceled yet), rather than wrongly counting them as failures or throwing them out.
leaves.intuition: At each time an event occurs, compute the fraction of those "still at risk" who experience the event, then multiply together the survival fractions across time points. Censored individuals (e.g., customers who haven't churned yet) stay in the risk set until they leave observation, so survival time is not underestimated.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)$
$d_i$ is the number of events at time $t_i$
$n_i$ is the number still at risk just before that time
Group comparison: log-rank test
assumptions: Censoring is unrelated to the event (non-informative censoring)
Individuals who enter observation at different times have the same survival probabilities
checks: Plot each group's curve with confidence bands
Check the proportion of and reasons for censoring (e.g., whether dropout is related to the outcome)
pros: Handles censored data correctly
Nonparametric, intuitive survival curves
use: Customer retention and time-to-churn analysis
Time to policy lapse or equipment failure
Survival comparisons in clinical trials
cons: Cannot adjust for multiple covariates at once (requires a Cox model)
Unstable estimates in the tail, where few subjects remain
hp: Log-rank test (most powerful when proportional hazards hold)
Median survival time and survival rates at specific time points
With multiple event types, use the cumulative incidence function instead
leaves.tools: Python: lifelines.KaplanMeierFitter; R: survival::survfit

leaves.name: Cox Proportional Hazards Model
leaves.plain: Analyzes which factors make an event (churn, failure, death) happen "sooner." Results are read as hazard ratios, for example: "the churn risk on a monthly plan is 1.8 times that on an annual plan." You don't have to specify how the baseline risk evolves over time, but the model assumes the hazard ratio stays constant over time.
leaves.intuition: It models the instantaneous risk (hazard): each person's hazard = a shared baseline hazard × exp(covariate effects). The clever part is that you can estimate the relative effects of the covariates (hazard ratios) without specifying what the baseline hazard looks like.
leaves.objective:
$h(t \mid X) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp(X\beta)$
Partial likelihood: $L(\beta) = \prod_{\text{event } i} \frac{\exp(x_i \beta)}{\sum_{j \in R(t_i)} \exp(x_j \beta)}$
$\exp(\beta_j)$ is the hazard ratio
assumptions: Proportional hazards: covariate effects do not change over time
Non-informative censoring
Covariates are linearly related to the log hazard
checks: Test the proportional hazards assumption with Schoenfeld residuals
Check whether the log(−log S(t)) curves are parallel
Check the functional form with martingale residuals
pros: Semiparametric: no need to specify the baseline hazard
Intuitive hazard ratios
Can include time-varying covariates
use: Risk factor analysis for customer churn
Time to credit default
Insurance claims and policy lapse
cons: The proportional hazards assumption is often violated
A hazard ratio is not a difference in survival time and is easily misunderstood when communicated
hp: Add interactions with time, or use a stratified Cox model
Predicting survival probabilities requires separately estimating the baseline hazard
leaves.tools: Python: lifelines.CoxPHFitter; R: survival::coxph

children.name: Causal Inference
children.signal: The target quantity is an interventional effect P(Y | do(X)): what would happen to the outcome if the treatment were changed. The core difficulty is not estimation but "identification": under what assumptions the data can answer a counterfactual question.
children.criterion: L2 split criterion: how the treatment is assigned (randomized by the researcher / determined by an exogenous rule or event / self-selected by units)

children.name: Randomized Experiments
children.def: The researcher assigns the treatment at random. Randomization guarantees that the groups are comparable, so identification needs no additional assumptions; the challenges lie in designing and running the experiment.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the main challenge the experiment must overcome (basic assignment / too much noise / interference between units / need for early stopping)

children.name: Basic Randomized Designs
children.philosophy: The researcher controls assignment: randomness severs the link between the treatment and all confounders (including unobserved ones), so differences between groups can come only from the treatment.

leaves.name: A/B Testing (with SRM Check)
leaves.plain: Randomly split users into groups A and B that differ only in the change being tested, then compare outcomes. Because assignment is random, the two groups are alike on average in every other respect, so any difference can be attributed to the change. After launch, first check that the group sizes match the design (SRM); a mismatched ratio means the traffic split is broken and the results can't be trusted.
leaves.intuition: Random assignment makes the two groups "equal in expectation" on every characteristic, known and unknown, so any difference in outcomes can only come from the treatment itself. It is the only method that identifies causal effects without additional assumptions. The SRM (sample ratio mismatch) check verifies that the traffic split actually ran as designed: if a 50/50 experiment shows 50.8/49.2 on a large sample, that usually points to a bug in assignment or logging, and the results cannot be trusted.
leaves.objective:
$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)]$
Estimator: $\hat{\tau} = \bar{Y}_T - \bar{Y}_C$
$\operatorname{SE}(\hat{\tau}) = \sqrt{\frac{s_T^2}{n_T} + \frac{s_C^2}{n_C}}$
SRM check: $\chi^2 = \sum_{k} \frac{(O_k - E_k)^2}{E_k}$; flag if $p < 0.001$
assumptions: Randomization is correctly executed (no SRM)
SUTVA: no interference between units, and only one version of the treatment
Unit of analysis matches the unit of randomization
No contamination from other changes during the experiment
checks: SRM chi-square test
A/A tests: validate the platform's Type I error rate
Balance checks on pre-experiment metrics
Novelty effects: whether the effect decays over time
pros: The gold standard for causal identification
Simple analysis and easy-to-communicate results
Can be scaled up as a platform
use: Product features and UI redesigns
Pricing and promotion tests
Online evaluation of recommendation algorithms
cons: Some treatments can't be randomized (ethics, regulation, cost)
Network effects or shared resources violate SUTVA
Looking only at the average effect can mask heterogeneity
Short-term metrics don't necessarily reflect long-term value
hp: Set it in advance with a power analysis; don't stop as soon as you see significance
Pre-specify one overall evaluation criterion (OEC), plus guardrail metrics
When randomizing by user but measuring a ratio such as click-through rate, compute the variance with the delta method
Cover at least one full cycle (usually 1–2 weeks) to remove day-of-week effects
leaves.tools: Platforms: GrowthBook, Eppo, Statsig, Optimizely; Python: statsmodels, scipy.stats; R: estimatr

leaves.name: Stratified / Block Randomization
leaves.plain: First divide subjects into strata by important characteristics (e.g., new vs. returning customers, country), then randomize separately within each stratum. This ensures the two groups are fully balanced on those key characteristics and reduces differences due to luck, making results more precise. It is especially useful with small samples.
leaves.intuition: First split the sample into blocks by important covariates (region, new vs. returning customers), then randomize separately within each block. The two groups are then "guaranteed" to be balanced on these variables, not merely balanced in expectation; between-block variation is also removed from the error, which makes this especially effective in small experiments.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\tau} = \sum_{b} \frac{n_b}{n} \cdot \big(\bar{Y}_{T,b} - \bar{Y}_{C,b}\big)$
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}) = \sum_{b} \left(\frac{n_b}{n}\right)^2 \cdot \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_b)$
assumptions: Stratification variables are fixed before the experiment and unaffected by treatment
Each block has enough treatment and control units
Randomization within blocks is correctly executed
checks: Whether the treatment share in each stratum matches the design
Account for stratification in the analysis (stratum fixed effects); otherwise standard errors will be conservative
Whether any stratum has too few units
pros: Guarantees balance on key variables
Reduces estimator variance and increases power
Naturally yields stratum-level effects
use: Small-sample experiments (B2B clients, stores)
Experiments with strong predictors
Clinical trials (stratified by hospital)
cons: Too many stratification variables leave too few units per stratum
More complex to implement than simple randomization
Limited gains in large online experiments (use CUPED or post-stratification instead)
hp: Choose 1–3 variables strongly correlated with the outcome
With very small samples, pair units 1:1 and then randomize
If you can't stratify in advance, apply post-stratification at the analysis stage
leaves.tools: R: randomizr::block_ra, blockTools; Python: randomize within strata yourself with groupby (sklearn StratifiedShuffleSplit can help)

children.name: Variance Reduction
children.philosophy: Randomization already guarantees unbiasedness; what remains is noise. Use pre-treatment information to explain away the predictable part of the outcome, so the same sample yields a narrower interval.

leaves.name: CUPED Variance Reduction
leaves.plain: People's outcomes differ a lot to begin with (heavy users buy more anyway), and that noise can drown out the experiment's effect. CUPED uses pre-experiment behavior to subtract the differences that "would have been there anyway," leaving only the part caused by the experiment. Variance drops sharply, so the same sample size gives more precise measurements and faster conclusions.
leaves.intuition: Users differ to begin with (heavy users spend more anyway); these differences are unrelated to the treatment but make outcomes highly variable. CUPED uses the same metric measured before the experiment as a covariate, subtracts the "already predictable part," and compares only what remains. Because the covariate is determined before treatment, it introduces no bias, yet the variance can drop substantially.
leaves.objective:
$\tilde{Y} = Y - \theta\,(X - \bar{X})$, $\theta = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y, X)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}$
$\operatorname{Var}(\tilde{Y}) = \operatorname{Var}(Y)\,(1 - \rho^2)$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between $X$ and $Y$
$\hat{\tau} = \bar{\tilde{Y}}_T - \bar{\tilde{Y}}_C$
assumptions: The covariate is measured before treatment and unaffected by it
Valid randomization
θ is estimated on the pooled sample (or via group-wise regression)
checks: Confirm that the covariate's time window precedes the start of the experiment
Compare point estimates before and after CUPED (they should not change much)
Estimate the fraction of variance removed, ρ²
pros: Increases power without more samples (variance roughly halves when ρ = 0.7)
Simple to implement; equivalent to regression adjustment
No change to the experimental design needed
use: Standard feature of online experimentation platforms
High-variance metrics (revenue, time spent)
Products dominated by existing users
cons: New users have no pre-experiment data
Limited benefit when the covariate is weakly correlated with the outcome
Mistakenly using post-treatment variables introduces bias
hp: Most often the same metric measured pre-experiment; multiple covariates or ML predictions (CUPAC) also work
Typically 1–4 weeks; too long a window weakens the correlation
Fill in 0 for new users and add an indicator variable
leaves.tools: Platforms: built into Eppo, Statsig, GrowthBook; Python: statsmodels OLS (Y ~ T + X_pre)
leaves.note: CUPED is mathematically equivalent to regression adjustment (Lin 2013: Y ~ T + X + T×X). It differs from "observational adjustment": randomization already guarantees unbiasedness, and the covariate only serves to reduce variance.

children.name: Interference & Network Effects
children.philosophy: When one unit's treatment affects others (violating SUTVA), raise the randomization unit to a level that interference does not cross: clusters, time periods, or markets.

leaves.name: Cluster Randomization
leaves.plain: Sometimes you can't randomize individuals (e.g., staff at the same store influence each other, students in the same class talk to one another), so you randomize whole groups (stores, classes, cities) instead. Keep in mind that the effective sample size is closer to the number of groups than to the number of people.
leaves.intuition: When individuals influence each other (the same circle of friends, the same store), individual-level randomization "contaminates" the control group. The fix is to assign entire clusters together. The cost is that people within a cluster are similar, so the effective sample size shrinks dramatically.
leaves.objective:
Design effect: $\text{DE} = 1 + (m - 1) \cdot \text{ICC}$, where $m$ is the average cluster size
Effective sample size: $n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n}{\text{DE}}$
Analysis: compare cluster-level means, or individual-level regression + cluster-robust standard errors
assumptions: Interference occurs only within clusters, not across them
Enough clusters (at least 20–30 per arm recommended)
Clusters are defined before the experiment and unaffected by treatment
checks: Estimate the ICC and compute the design effect
Check for spillover between clusters (whether neighboring clusters affect each other)
With few clusters, use small-sample corrections or randomization inference
pros: Handles network effects and contamination
Matches many real-world units of assignment (stores, cities, schools)
use: Social feature experiments (clustered by social circle)
Store or regional marketing campaigns
Two-sided marketplaces (assigned by city)
cons: Substantial loss of power
Unstable inference with few clusters
Unequal cluster sizes increase variance
hp: Trade off keeping interference contained within clusters against having enough clusters
Must use cluster-robust standard errors; otherwise the Type I error rate is badly inflated
Use the wild cluster bootstrap or randomization inference
leaves.tools: Python: statsmodels (cov_type='cluster'), linearmodels; R: estimatr::lm_robust(clusters =), clubSandwich

leaves.name: Switchback Experiment
leaves.plain: In two-sided marketplaces (food delivery, ride-hailing), the treatment and control groups compete for the same pool of drivers and interfere with each other. A switchback experiment instead uses "time slot × region" as the unit, turning the new policy on and off in turns and comparing performance in the on and off periods, so the two groups don't contaminate each other.
leaves.intuition: In two-sided marketplaces like food delivery and ride-hailing, all users share the same pool of drivers, so any experiment that splits users suffers from interference. A switchback experiment randomizes "time" instead: the whole market uses A in some time slots and B in others, alternating at random, and each time slot is one experimental unit.
leaves.objective:
Time slot $t$ is randomly assigned $W_t \in \{A, B\}$
$\hat{\tau} = \text{mean}(Y_t \mid W_t = B)$
$\qquad - \text{mean}(Y_t \mid W_t = A)$
Carryover effects: discard the first $k$ periods after each switch (burn-in)
assumptions: Carryover effects are limited and shorter than the time slot
No other systematic differences between time slots (or they are controlled for with time fixed effects)
The treatment can be switched instantly
checks: Whether carryover effects appear in the first few periods after a switch
Whether estimates are stable across different slot lengths
Autocorrelation of slot-level residuals
pros: Addresses market-level interference
Does not require multiple independent markets
use: Dispatch and pricing algorithms for delivery and ride-hailing
Inventory and logistics strategies
Ad bidding strategies
cons: Limited number of time slots, so power is usually low
Carryover effects cause bias
Slot length is hard to choose
hp: Longer than the carryover effect, yet short enough to yield enough slots (commonly 30 minutes to a few hours)
Switch multiple cities simultaneously to increase the sample
Use randomization inference (permutation) or HAC standard errors
leaves.tools: Mostly built in-house; Python: statsmodels (HAC standard errors), a hand-written permutation test; see the methodology posts published by DoorDash and Lyft

children.name: Continuous Monitoring & Early Stopping
children.philosophy: Experimental results accumulate over time. If you want to look at interim results and decide whether to stop, the "repeated looks" themselves must be built into Type I error control.

leaves.name: Sequential Testing (Always-Valid / α-Spending)
leaves.plain: A traditional test lets you look at the results only once, at a pre-set sample size; peeking repeatedly and stopping as soon as something looks significant greatly raises the chance of a false alarm. Sequential testing sets up rules in advance that let you look at any time, so you can stop an experiment early while still keeping false alarms under control.
leaves.intuition: If you check the p-value every day and stop the moment it is significant, the actual Type I error rate will be far above 5% (every extra look is effectively another test). Sequential testing plans in advance "how many looks, and how much α to spend at each," or uses confidence sequences that are valid at any time, so you can legitimately stop early.
leaves.objective:
O'Brien–Fleming-type $\alpha$ spending:
$\alpha(t) = 2 - 2\Phi\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt{t}}\right)$, where $t$ is the fraction of information accrued so far
mSPRT: $\Lambda_n = \int \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{f_\theta(x_i)}{f_{\theta_0}(x_i)}\, dH(\theta)$
Reject the null hypothesis when $\Lambda_n \ge 1/\alpha$
assumptions: The number of looks is planned in advance, or an always-valid method is used
Independent observations (or dependence accounted for)
Data are real-time and accurate
checks: Confirm the actual Type I error rate by simulation
Whether effect estimates are inflated when stopping early (winner's curse)
Whether the planned information fractions match the actual ones
pros: Legitimate early stopping saves traffic and time
Allows continuously monitored dashboards
use: Real-time monitoring on online experimentation platforms
Interim analyses in clinical trials
Real-time alerts on guardrail metrics
cons: Lower power than a fixed-sample test
Effect estimates are inflated when stopping early
More complex to implement and communicate
hp: Group sequential for a few interim analyses; mSPRT or confidence sequences for continuous monitoring
O'Brien–Fleming is conservative early and lenient late; Pocock spends α evenly
The scale of the mixing distribution should be close to the expected effect size
leaves.tools: R: gsDesign, rpact; Python: spotify-confidence; Platforms: Optimizely Stats Engine, Eppo, Statsig
leaves.note: Methodologically it is a hypothesis test, but in practice it is used almost exclusively to decide when to stop an experiment, so it is filed under randomized experiments according to its most typical use.

children.name: Quasi-experimental Designs
children.def: The treatment is not assigned by the researcher but determined by an external rule, timing, or event, which creates "as-good-as-random" variation. Identification rests on defensible design assumptions.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the source of exogenous variation (time × group / score threshold / exogenous instrument / time-series break point)

children.name: Panel Comparisons (Time × Group)
children.philosophy: When there are treatment and control groups with data from before and after treatment, use the control group's change to infer how the treatment group would have changed "without the treatment."

leaves.name: Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
leaves.plain: Comparing only before vs. after a launch mixes in the overall trend; comparing only the treatment and control groups mixes in differences the two groups already had. DiD subtracts one difference from the other: the treatment group's before-after change minus the control group's before-after change. As long as "the two groups would have followed the same trend without treatment," what remains is the treatment effect.
leaves.intuition: Comparing only before vs. after a launch mixes in the overall trend; comparing only the treatment and control groups mixes in differences the two groups already had. DiD subtracts one difference from the other: the treatment group's before-after change − the control group's before-after change. As long as "the two groups would have followed the same trend without treatment," what remains is the treatment effect.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\tau} = (\bar{Y}_{T,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{T,\text{pre}})$
$\qquad - (\bar{Y}_{C,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{C,\text{pre}})$
Regression form (two-way fixed effects):
$Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$
assumptions: Parallel trends: absent treatment, the two groups would follow the same trend
No anticipation: pre-treatment behavior is unaffected by the upcoming treatment
Stable composition, with no selective entry or exit
The control group is unaffected by treatment spillovers
checks: Plot pre-treatment trends
Event-study plot: pre-treatment coefficients should be close to 0
Placebo tests: fake treatment timing or fake treatment groups
Check whether conclusions agree with the outcome in logs vs. levels
pros: Intuitive and easy to communicate
Removes time-invariant differences between groups
Needs only panel or repeated cross-section data
use: New features or policies rolled out by region
Impact of regulatory changes
Regional evaluation of marketing campaigns
cons: Parallel trends cannot be tested directly
Low credibility when the two groups differ substantially
With staggered rollout, two-way fixed effects are biased (see Staggered DiD)
hp: Cluster-robust standard errors at the level of treatment assignment (e.g., city)
Pick units with the most similar pre-treatment trends, or combine with matching or synthetic control
Include only pre-treatment covariates to avoid bad controls
leaves.tools: Python: linearmodels PanelOLS, pyfixest, statsmodels; R: fixest, did

leaves.name: Staggered DiD / Event Study
leaves.plain: The policy or feature rolls out in waves (city A first, city B later). Traditional DiD uses the early groups, which are already affected, as controls for the later groups, producing biased or even reversed answers. Newer methods use only groups that "haven't been treated yet" as controls, and can chart how the effect evolves over time after launch.
leaves.intuition: When units adopt treatment at different times, conventional two-way fixed effects use "already-treated units" as controls for later adopters. If effects change over time, this produces wrong or even negative weights, and the estimate can get even the sign wrong. The new methods use only "not-yet-treated" or "never-treated" units as controls, estimate cohort by cohort, and then aggregate.
leaves.objective:
Cohort × time effects (Callaway–Sant'Anna):
$\text{ATT}(g, t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid G = g]$
$\qquad - \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid \text{not yet treated}]$
Event-study aggregation: $\theta(e) = \sum_{g} w_g \cdot \text{ATT}(g, g + e)$
$e$ is time relative to launch
assumptions: Conditional parallel trends (holding for every cohort)
No anticipation
Irreversible treatment (no switching off after launch)
A never-treated or not-yet-treated control group exists
checks: Goodman-Bacon decomposition: how much of the TWFE weight comes from "already-treated units as controls"
Pre-treatment coefficients in the event-study plot
Agreement across estimators (Callaway–Sant'Anna, Sun–Abraham, imputation)
pros: Corrects TWFE bias under heterogeneous effects
Estimates how effects evolve over time
Makes full use of the variation from staggered rollout
use: Products launched city by city
Regulations taking effect at different times across regions
Internal policies rolled out in phases
cons: More complex estimators that need a reasonable sample size
Unstable estimates when cohorts are small
Still relies on parallel trends
hp: Never-treated units are cleaner; not-yet-treated units give a larger sample
Aggregate by cohort, by calendar time, or by event time
Event studies usually use e = −1 as the baseline
leaves.tools: Python: csdid, differences, pyfixest; R: did, fixest::sunab, didimputation, bacondecomp
leaves.note: If you still want a regression-based event study, use the interaction-weighted estimator of Sun & Abraham (2021) rather than conventional TWFE with lead and lag dummies.

leaves.name: Synthetic Control
leaves.plain: When only one unit is treated (say, a city launches a new policy), there is no perfect comparison city. Synthetic control blends several untreated cities with weights into a virtual twin "whose pre-policy trajectory is almost identical to the treated city"; after the policy, the gap between the two is the effect.
leaves.intuition: With a single treated unit (e.g., one city), a perfect control is hard to find. Synthetic control uses a weighted average of multiple control units to "assemble" a synthetic control whose pre-treatment trajectory nearly matches the treated unit; the post-treatment gap between the two is the effect.
leaves.objective:
Weights: $w^* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{w} \lVert X_1 - X_0 w \rVert_V$
Subject to $w_j \ge 0$, $\sum_{j} w_j = 1$
Effect: $\hat{\tau}_t = Y_{1t} - \sum_{j} w_j^* \cdot Y_{jt}$, $t > T_0$
assumptions: The treated unit lies within the convex hull of the control units (can be approximated by a weighted average)
A long enough pre-treatment period with good fit
Control units are unaffected by spillovers
No other shocks during the treatment period that affect only the treated unit
checks: Pre-treatment fit error (RMSPE)
Placebo tests: treat each control unit in turn as the treated unit
Use the rank of the post/pre-treatment RMSPE ratio as a p-value
Leave-one-out: drop the control unit with the largest weight
pros: Suited to settings with only one or a few treated units
Transparent, interpretable weights
Does not require parallel trends
use: Policy evaluation for a single city or country
Brand campaigns in a single market
Regional impact of major events (e.g., a new store opening)
cons: Inference relies mainly on permutation tests, so p-value granularity is limited by the number of control units
Not credible when the pre-treatment fit is poor
Cannot fit a treated unit that is an extreme outlier
hp: Exclude units that may be affected by spillovers
Pre-treatment outcome values at multiple time points matter most
