Synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021) combines DiD and synthetic control and is usually more robust
leaves.tools: Python: pysyncon, SparseSC, CausalPy; R: Synth, tidysynth, synthdid

children.name: Threshold Rules
children.philosophy: Treatment is determined by whether a continuous score crosses a threshold. Units just on either side of the threshold are approximately randomly assigned.

leaves.name: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
leaves.plain: When eligibility is set by a cutoff (a score of 60 to pass, spending NT$1,000 to be upgraded), people just above and just below the line are essentially the same; luck simply put them on different sides. Comparing people on either side of the cutoff amounts to a natural randomized experiment.
leaves.intuition: When treatment is determined by a score cutoff (a card is approved only if the credit score is ≥ 650; free shipping only above a minimum spend), people just on either side of the cutoff are nearly identical and differ only in whether they were treated. Comparing people very close to either side of the cutoff is like a local randomized experiment.
leaves.objective:
Sharp RD: $\tau = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$
$\qquad - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$
Estimation: fit a local linear regression on each side within bandwidth $h$ and take the difference in intercepts
Fuzzy RD: $\tau = \frac{\text{jump in outcome at cutoff}}{\text{jump in treatment probability at cutoff}}$
assumptions: Conditional expectations of the potential outcomes are continuous at the cutoff
Individuals cannot precisely manipulate the score (cannot just squeeze past the cutoff)
No other policy changes at the same cutoff
checks: Density test (McCrary/rddensity): is there bunching at the cutoff?
Continuity of pre-treatment covariates at the cutoff
Placebo cutoffs
Bandwidth sensitivity analysis
pros: High internal validity, close to a randomized experiment
Intuitive, persuasive graphics
use: Card-approval or credit-limit policies with credit-score cutoffs
Effects of benefits at membership-tier thresholds
Free-shipping thresholds and subsidy-eligibility cutoffs
cons: Identifies only the local effect near the cutoff
Few observations near the cutoff, so power is low
Breaks down when the score can be manipulated
hp: Use the MSE-optimal bandwidth (rdrobust selects it automatically)
Use local linear fits, not high-order global polynomials
leaves.tools: Python: rdrobust, rddensity; R: rdrobust, rddensity, rdd

children.name: Exogenous Instruments
children.philosophy: Find an exogenous variable that affects the outcome only through the treatment, and estimate the effect using only the part of the treatment variation that it induces.

leaves.name: Instrumental Variables (2SLS)
leaves.plain: You want the effect of X on Y, but X and Y may both be driven by factors you cannot see. So you find an outside factor that "affects Y only through X" (an instrumental variable), such as distance to a college affecting whether someone goes to college. Using only the part of the variation in X that the instrument drives gives a clean estimate of the causal effect.
leaves.intuition: If treatment and outcome are both affected by unobserved factors, a direct regression is biased. Find an exogenous variable Z (the instrument) that "affects the outcome only through the treatment," and estimate using only the part of the treatment variation induced by Z. A common example: randomly sent encouragement messages (Z) → actual feature usage (D) → retention (Y).
leaves.objective:
First stage: $D = \pi_0 + \pi_1 Z + \nu$
Second stage: $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{D} + \varepsilon$
Single binary instrument (Wald): $\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y, Z)}{\operatorname{Cov}(D, Z)}$
Under heterogeneous effects, $\beta_1$ is the local average treatment effect (LATE) for "compliers"
assumptions: Relevance: Z has a sufficiently strong effect on D
Exclusion restriction: Z affects Y only through D
Independence: Z is unrelated to the potential outcomes (as good as random)
Monotonicity: no "defiers" (needed for the LATE interpretation)
checks: First-stage F-statistic (conventional threshold of 10; recent work recommends stricter ones)
Anderson–Rubin test: inference that remains valid with weak instruments
Overidentification test (Hansen J) with multiple instruments
Argue for the exclusion restriction with theory and placebo outcomes
pros: Handles unobserved confounders
Handles imperfect compliance in experiments
use: Encouragement designs (randomized encouragement)
Imperfect compliance in experiments (assigned to group B but did not use the feature)
Demand estimation (cost shocks as instruments for price)
cons: Good instruments are hard to find
The exclusion restriction cannot be fully verified
Weak instruments cause large bias and unreliable intervals
LATE does not necessarily equal the overall ATE
hp: Randomized encouragement, exogenous policy or geographic variation, institutional rules
Use robust or clustered standard errors
When the F-statistic is low, switch to Anderson–Rubin intervals or LIML
leaves.tools: Python: linearmodels IV2SLS, statsmodels; R: fixest (IV syntax in feols), ivreg, AER

children.name: Interrupted Time Series
children.philosophy: When there is no contemporaneous control, use the pre-treatment temporal pattern and related series unaffected by the treatment to predict the counterfactual path "had there been no treatment."

leaves.name: Interrupted Time Series / CausalImpact
leaves.plain: Use this when you have only one unit but a long time series. The pre-intervention trajectory is used to predict "what would have happened without the intervention," which is then compared with what actually happened; the gap is the effect. CausalImpact can also bring in related series unaffected by the intervention to improve forecast accuracy.
leaves.intuition: When a change launches to everyone with no concurrent control group, use the pre-treatment time series (plus related, unaffected series) to forecast "what would have happened without the change," and compare it with the actual values. CausalImpact makes this forecast with a Bayesian structural time-series model and reports credible intervals.
leaves.objective:
Segmented regression:
$Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 D_t$
$\qquad + \beta_3 (t - T_0) D_t + \varepsilon_t$
($\beta_2$: level change, $\beta_3$: slope change)
CausalImpact: fit on pre-treatment data
$Y_t = \mu_t + \gamma_t + \beta^\top x_t + \varepsilon_t$ (trend + seasonality + control series)
Effect: $\hat{\tau}_t = Y_t - \hat{Y}_t$ ($\hat{Y}_t$ is the counterfactual prediction)
assumptions: Absent treatment, the pre-treatment pattern would have continued
Control series are unaffected by the treatment
A well-defined treatment time with no other concurrent shocks
A sufficiently long pre-treatment period
checks: Hold out a pre-treatment window for backtesting (forecast error)
Placebo treatment dates
Pre-treatment correlation between the control series and the outcome
pros: No concurrent control group needed
Shows how the effect accumulates over time
CausalImpact directly outputs counterfactual plots and intervals
use: Redesigns or brand campaigns launched to everyone
Estimating the impact of system outages or external events
Natural experiments in search and traffic
cons: Cannot rule out other concurrent events
Uncertainty grows with the length of the forecast horizon
Sensitive to model specification
hp: Cover at least several seasonal cycles
Pick series correlated with the outcome but unaffected by treatment (other markets, other categories)
Segmented regression needs Newey–West standard errors or ARIMA errors
leaves.tools: R: CausalImpact, bsts; Python: tfcausalimpact, statsmodels

children.name: Observational Adjustment
children.def: Units select their own treatment, and no exogenous variation is available. All one can do is assume that "the measured covariates capture all confounders" (conditional exchangeability) and then adjust via modeling or weighting.
children.criterion: L3 split criterion: the target estimand (an overall average effect, ATE/ATT, or an individualized conditional effect, CATE)

children.name: Average-Effect Adjustment
children.philosophy: Make the treatment and control groups comparable on measured covariates, then estimate the overall average effect. Methods can be further divided by what is modeled: the outcome only (G-computation), the treatment only (matching, IPW), or both (AIPW, DML).

leaves.name: Regression Adjustment / G-computation
leaves.plain: Use a model to answer: "If everyone received the treatment, what would the average outcome be? And if no one did?" The difference between the two is the effect. The premise is that every factor that affects both "whether someone is treated" and "the outcome" has been observed and included in the model.
leaves.intuition: First fit an outcome model E[Y | T, X], then ask: "If everyone were treated, what would the average outcome be? And if no one were?" Predict for every individual under both treatment states, take the difference, and average. It generalizes "standardization," and any predictive model can serve as the outcome model.
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\mu}_t(x) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y \mid T = t, X = x]$
$\widehat{\text{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big[\hat{\mu}_1(X_i) - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i)\big]$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding): Y(t) ⊥ T | X
Positivity (overlap): 0 < P(T = 1 | X) < 1
Consistency: the observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment actually received
Correctly specified outcome model
checks: Draw a causal diagram (DAG) to settle the adjustment set
Degree of covariate overlap between the two groups
Sensitivity analysis (E-value): how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the conclusion
Check the outcome model's predictive performance with cross-validation
pros: Conceptually intuitive; works with any predictive model
Efficient when the model is correct
Subgroup effects are easy to estimate
use: ATE estimation from observational data
Paired with the bootstrap to produce intervals
Time-varying treatments (G-formula)
cons: Biased if the outcome model is misspecified
Relies on model extrapolation when overlap is poor
Standard errors require the bootstrap
hp: Linear, GLM, or ML; with ML, prefer AIPW or DML instead
Include only confounders, never mediators or colliders
leaves.tools: Python: DoWhy, causalml, zEpid; R: marginaleffects, stdReg
leaves.note: How it differs from ordinary OLS: the OLS treatment coefficient equals the ATE only when there are no interactions; G-computation predicts first and then averages, so it still recovers the ATE with interactions or nonlinear models.

leaves.name: Propensity Score Matching (PSM)
tasks: Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT)
leaves.plain: In observational data, people who received the treatment differ from those who did not to begin with. First estimate each person's "probability of being treated" (the propensity score), then pair each treated person with an untreated person of similar probability, so the two groups become comparable on observed characteristics.
leaves.intuition: Matching on many covariates at once is hard. Rosenbaum and Rubin showed that matching on the "probability of treatment" (the propensity score) alone is enough to balance covariates between the groups. So for each treated unit, find an untreated unit with a similar propensity score, then compare their outcomes.
leaves.objective:
Propensity score: $e(X) = \mathbb{P}(T = 1 \mid X)$
Matching: for each treated unit $i$, find
$j = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{j \in \text{control}} \big|\operatorname{logit} \hat{e}(X_i) - \operatorname{logit} \hat{e}(X_j)\big|$
with distance within the caliper
$\widehat{\text{ATT}} = \frac{1}{n_T} \sum_{i \in \text{treated}} \big(Y_i - Y_{j(i)}\big)$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding)
Positivity: control observations exist across the treated group's propensity-score range
The propensity score model balances the covariates
checks: Standardized mean differences after matching (SMD < 0.1)
Overlap plot of propensity score distributions
Share of treated observations discarded (changes the population the effect represents)
Sensitivity analysis (Rosenbaum bounds)
pros: Intuitive; matched data are easy to understand and communicate
Separates design from outcome analysis (balance first, then look at outcomes)
use: Observational studies in medicine and policy
Evaluating self-selected treatments such as membership programs or course participation
Post hoc evaluation of marketing campaigns
cons: Discards unmatched observations, losing information
King & Nielsen (2019) show that PSM can actually increase imbalance and model dependence
Variance estimation after matching is more complex
hp: Commonly 0.2 standard deviations of the logit propensity score
1:1 or 1:k, with or without replacement; CEM or optimal matching are also worth considering
leaves.tools: R: MatchIt, cobalt; Python: causalml, psmpy, DoWhy

leaves.name: Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW)
leaves.plain: Instead of matching, reweight: the less a treated person "looks like someone who would be treated" (that is, the rarer they are), the larger their weight, so that after weighting the two groups' characteristics look as if treatment had been randomly assigned. Beware: extreme weights can make the estimate very unstable.
leaves.intuition: In observational data, some people are more likely to be treated than others. IPW gives larger weights to people who were "unlikely to be treated but were treated anyway" and smaller weights to those who were "very likely to be treated." Reweighting yields a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of the covariates, just as under random assignment.
leaves.objective:
$\widehat{\text{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[\frac{T_i Y_i}{\hat{e}(X_i)} - \frac{(1 - T_i)\, Y_i}{1 - \hat{e}(X_i)}\right]$
Stabilized weights: $w_i = \frac{\mathbb{P}(T = T_i)}{\mathbb{P}(T = T_i \mid X_i)}$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability
Positivity: propensity scores are not close to 0 or 1
Correctly specified propensity score model
checks: Weight distribution (maximum weight, effective sample size)
Covariate balance after weighting (SMD)
Propensity score overlap plot
Compare results before and after trimming
pros: No outcome model required
Keeps all observations
Extends easily to time-varying treatments (marginal structural models)
use: ATE/ATT estimation from observational data
Handling selection bias and missing data
Offline evaluation of recommendation policies (off-policy evaluation)
cons: Extreme weights can blow up the variance
Biased if the propensity score model is misspecified
Standard errors require robust estimation or the bootstrap
hp: Truncate propensity scores to [0.01, 0.99], or drop observations outside the region of overlap
Use stabilized weights or Hájek normalization
Tune it for "covariate balance," not predictive accuracy
leaves.tools: R: WeightIt, cobalt, ipw; Python: causalml, DoWhy, zEpid

leaves.name: Doubly Robust Estimation (AIPW)
leaves.plain: Build two models at once, one that predicts the outcome and one that predicts who gets treated, then combine them. As long as either model is right, the estimate will not be biased. It is like buying double insurance, hence the name "doubly robust."
leaves.intuition: Combines an outcome model with a propensity score model: predict with the outcome model, then use IPW to correct the outcome model's residuals. The estimate is consistent as long as "either one" of the two models is correct, hence "doubly robust." It is also the theoretical foundation for using ML in causal estimation (DML, TMLE).
leaves.objective:
$\hat{\psi} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigg[\hat{\mu}_1(X_i) - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i)$
$\qquad + \frac{T_i\,(Y_i - \hat{\mu}_1(X_i))}{\hat{e}(X_i)}$
$\qquad - \frac{(1 - T_i)\,(Y_i - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i))}{1 - \hat{e}(X_i)}\bigg]$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability
Positivity
At least one of the outcome model and the propensity model is correct
checks: Propensity score overlap and weight distribution
Cross-validated performance of each model
Compare the estimate with IPW and G-computation
pros: Doubly robust
Attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both models are correct
Works with ML models (requires cross-fitting)
use: The go-to ATE estimator for observational data
Policy evaluation
Off-policy evaluation (doubly robust OPE)
cons: Still biased when both models are wrong
Extreme propensity scores still cause instability
Cross-fitting is mandatory with ML

leaves.name: Double Machine Learning (DML)
leaves.plain: You want to use machine learning to control for a large number of confounders and still get a causal estimate with a confidence interval. The approach: first use ML to strip out the confounders' influence on the "treatment" and on the "outcome" separately, then estimate the effect from what is left, using cross-fitting to avoid bias from overfitting.
leaves.intuition: With many confounders and nonlinear relationships, you want ML to do the adjustment; but plugging ML straight into a regression lets regularization bias contaminate the treatment effect. DML works "residual on residual": use ML to remove the part of Y and of T that X can explain, then run a simple regression of one residual on the other; combined with cross-fitting, this yields valid confidence intervals.
leaves.objective:
Partially linear model: $Y = \theta T + g(X) + \varepsilon$
$T = m(X) + \nu$
$\tilde{Y} = Y - \hat{\ell}(X)$, $\tilde{T} = T - \hat{m}(X)$
($\hat{\ell}$, $\hat{m}$ estimated by cross-fitting)
$\hat{\theta} = \frac{\sum_{i} \tilde{T}_i \tilde{Y}_i}{\sum_{i} \tilde{T}_i^2}$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability (all confounders are in X)
Positivity: enough residual variation in treatment after controlling for X
Both nuisance models converge fast enough (product of rates faster than $n^{-1/2}$)
checks: Cross-validated performance of the nuisance models
Whether the treatment residual T̃ has enough variation
Whether the estimate is stable across different ML learners
Repeat the sample splitting several times and take the median
pros: Controls high-dimensional confounding with any ML model
√n-consistent, asymptotically normal estimates with confidence intervals
Unified theoretical foundation (Neyman orthogonality)
use: Estimating price elasticities and marketing effects
Effect estimation that controls for many user characteristics
Combined with instrumental variables (DML-IV)
cons: Still relies on "no unmeasured confounding"
Sensitive to the choice of learners and hyperparameters
Higher computational cost
hp: K = 5 is common; repeat the splitting several times and take the median
GBDT, random forest, or Lasso, depending on the data
PLR (partially linear) or IRM (interactive model, suited to binary treatments)
leaves.tools: Python: DoubleML, EconML (LinearDML); R: DoubleML

children.name: Heterogeneous Effects (CATE)
children.philosophy: Ask not only "does it work on average?" but "for whom does it work, and how much?": learn the treatment effect itself as a function of X, directly supporting personalized decisions.

leaves.name: Meta-learners (S/T/X)
leaves.plain: The goal is to estimate "how large the effect is for different people" (heterogeneous effects), to find who most deserves to be treated. The S-learner uses one model with treatment as a feature; the T-learner builds a separate model for the treatment and control groups and takes the difference; the X-learner works better when the two groups differ greatly in size.
leaves.intuition: Assemble individualized effects from off-the-shelf ML models. The S-learner treats treatment as just another feature and trains a single model; the T-learner trains separate models for the treatment and control groups and subtracts them; the X-learner first estimates each individual's effect, then combines the estimates with propensity-score weights, and is especially effective when the treatment and control groups are very unequal in size.
leaves.objective:
Target: $\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]$
S: $\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}(x, 1) - \hat{\mu}(x, 0)$
T: $\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)$
X: $\tilde{D}_i^{1} = Y_i - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i)$, $\tilde{D}_i^{0} = \hat{\mu}_1(X_i) - Y_i$
Fit each separately to obtain $\hat{\tau}_1$ and $\hat{\tau}_0$
$\hat{\tau}(x) = e(x)\, \hat{\tau}_0(x) + (1 - e(x))\, \hat{\tau}_1(x)$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability (randomized experiment data are ideal)
Positivity
The base learners can capture the outcome functions
checks: Qini/AUUC curves (uplift ranking ability)
Group by predicted CATE and check whether the actual effects are monotonic across groups
Agreement across different learners
pros: Can use any ML model
Simple to implement, with mature packages
Directly supports targeting decisions
use: Uplift marketing (finding the "persuadables")
Personalized discounts and recommendations
Treatment allocation under a limited budget
cons: The S-learner tends to regularize the treatment effect toward 0
The T-learner has high variance with imbalanced samples
CATE has no ground-truth labels, so evaluation is hard
hp: Use the X-learner when treatment shares are very unbalanced; avoid the S-learner when effects are small
Use Qini curves, or check actual effects by CATE quantile
The R-learner and DR-learner have better theoretical properties
leaves.tools: Python: causalml, EconML, scikit-uplift; R: grf, rlearner

leaves.name: Causal Forest
leaves.plain: It turns a random forest into a tool built specifically to find "differences in effect": each split aims not to make predictions more accurate but to make the treatment effects of the two resulting groups differ as much as possible. The result tells you which segments see large effects and which see none, with confidence intervals, making it well suited to targeting.
leaves.intuition: A standard random forest splits on "reduction in prediction error"; a causal forest instead splits on "the difference in treatment effects between child nodes," so the people in each leaf respond similarly to treatment. Combined with "honest estimation" (half the sample determines the splits, the other half estimates the effects), it yields individualized effects with confidence intervals.
leaves.objective:
Split criterion: maximize $n_L \cdot n_R \cdot (\hat{\tau}_L - \hat{\tau}_R)^2$
Prediction: $\hat{\tau}(x) = \frac{\sum_{i} \alpha_i(x)\, \tilde{Y}_i \tilde{T}_i}{\sum_{i} \alpha_i(x)\, \tilde{T}_i^2}$
where $\tilde{Y}_i = Y_i - \hat{m}(X_i)$, $\tilde{T}_i = T_i - \hat{e}(X_i)$
$\alpha_i(x)$ is the similarity weight the forest assigns to observation $i$
assumptions: Conditional exchangeability
Positivity
Effects are locally smooth in feature space
checks: grf's test_calibration: whether the average effect and heterogeneity are correctly captured
AIPW effects by predicted-CATE group (RATE/TOC curves)
Variable importance: whether the features driving heterogeneity make sense
pros: Confidence intervals with theoretical guarantees
Discovers heterogeneity automatically
Extends to instrumental variables, survival, and quantiles (GRF framework)
use: Finding the customer segments that benefit most
Personalized policy allocation
Post-experiment heterogeneity analysis
cons: Requires large samples
Heterogeneity estimates are noisy in high dimensions
Interpreting the results still requires post hoc analysis
hp: Several thousand or more, for stable confidence intervals
Estimate Y.hat and W.hat first (grf does this by cross-fitting by default)
leaves.tools: R: grf; Python: EconML (CausalForestDML), causalml
